subject: Engineering Fundamentals
title: Reusable Rockets: Landing What You Launched
description: A fast breakdown of Reusable Rockets: Landing What You Launched for builders.

hook.text: SpaceX landed a Falcon 9 booster on a drone ship in 2016. Every aerospace engineer said it was nearly impossible.

buildup.text: Expendable rockets threw away $50 million boosters after each flight. Reusability could cut launch costs by 30 to 50 percent.

discovery.text: Landing requires saving fuel for the return burn. Grid fins steer the booster, and three engines reignite for the final descent.

twist.text: The Space Shuttle was reusable but cost more per launch than disposable rockets. Refurbishing between flights was very expensive.

climax.text: Falcon 9 boosters now fly over 20 times each. Starship aims for full reusability — both stages — at airline-like turnaround.

punchline.text: Why throw away a rocket when you can land it and fly again?

quiz.question: Why was the Space Shuttle's reusability less cost-effective than expected?
options: The shuttle could only be reused three times before structural fatigue
Refurbishment between flights was so expensive it cost more than expendable rockets
The shuttle's heat shield had to be completely replaced after each reentry
